rv.q: Elliot's production is polished and well-calibrated, the cast sharing great chemistry as well as occupying a complex matrix of audience appeal.

Elliott's production feels a bit fiddlier than it needs to be – Merle Hensel's distorting mirrored set is very clever but also quite distracting, and that's before you throw in the revolve and the odd bit of choreographed movement.
But it is Taron Egerton's M who makes the evening, with his phenomenal ability to combine comedy with desolation.
But while it works on its own terms, it's a difficult play to watch without an awareness of what it omits.

Terrific at conveying hurt, yearning and simmering self-doubt, Egerton now stars in Marianne Elliott’s revival of Mike Bartlett’s 2009 play Cock, a piece smartly and tragicomically about ongoing confusions of sexuality, the suffocating restrictions of categorisation and the agonies of the heart.
Its edge now lies in its theatrical repackaging by Marianne Elliott in this boldly stylised revival – with mixed results.
Whilst the title of Mike Bartlett’s 2009 play may intrigue and titillate some potential theatregoers, it may also deter others.
It's all terrifically clever and never dull as it unfolds over an unbroken hour and 45 minutes. But it is quite chilly.
It is a play that seems not quite complete but it is eminently watchable.
Unfortunately, this COCK isn't as titillating as its title seems to suggest. There are glimpses of pure passion and electricity, but there are also some overdone and tired tropes.
Those seeing Cock for its name, or the names attached to it, are in for a treat.
